authors.name: Rowan Vale
authors.bio: The man behind The Pecking Order. Rowan trades in sharp verdicts, spectacular reversals and an unwavering belief that this week finally explained everything. His inbox rarely agrees.

authors.name: Mara Voss
authors.bio: Mara follows the details that outlast the scoreboard: protection, personnel, responsibility and the choices that turn a talented roster into a contender.

authors.name: Ellis Quill
authors.bio: Ellis writes The Long Season, a column about the people and expectations beneath the standings. A bad afternoon is evidence, not a complete biography.

authors.name: Dorian Pike
authors.bio: Dorian asks the awkward question, counts the points and keeps asking. The Uncomfortable Truth takes the league’s overlooked clubs seriously.

authors.name: Tessa Wren
authors.bio: Tessa studies the matchups, names the pressure points and puts a score beside every pick. She covers the entire weekly slate for The Week Ahead.

authors.name: Calvin Rook
authors.bio: Calvin covers the college game and the next IFL class. The Rook Board is built around projection, athletic traits and the occasional prospect he refuses to stop believing in.

articles.title: Five touchdown passes end Cinnabar’s season—and my argument
articles.dek: Hatterene breaks a halftime tie with four second-half touchdowns as Blackthorn wins 38–10 and earns a trip to Mt. Silver.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: I picked Cinnabar. I thought its four-game winning streak, home field and capacity to make games uncomfortable would hold up against Blackthorn’s passing volume. At halftime, with the score 10–10, I still had a perfectly serviceable argument. Hatterene then spent the second half removing it, one completion at a time. The Dragons won 38–10, and the Blaze’s first postseason ended with twenty-eight unanswered points.

Hatterene finished 28 of 37 for 367 yards, five touchdowns and one interception. Hawlucha caught three of the scores. Simeon Ice caught the other two. Grovyle caught all nine passes thrown his way for 135 yards without reaching the end zone, which is a rather thorough way to participate in someone else’s touchdown montage. Blackthorn now visits Mt. Silver, the conference’s top seed, with an offense capable of making that trip considerably more interesting than the Reds might prefer.

Cinnabar’s loss deserves a precise account. The Blaze did not surrender a succession of defensive touchdowns or lose a pile of fumbles. Both teams threw one interception, and neither lost a fumble. The separation came from passing efficiency, third-down execution and the pressure Blackthorn applied when Cinnabar tried to answer. The Dragons converted four of eight third downs. The Blaze converted two of eleven. Those possessions became the second half’s governing fact.
A tie that disappeared in one quarter

We had a tied game at halftime and enough evidence that the passing opportunities were there. The receivers kept finishing their work. The next opponent gets to study every one of those touchdowns, so our preparation has to account for that instead of assuming the same openings will appear.
body.speaker: Clair

body.text: Hatterene opened the scoring with a twenty-yard touchdown pass deep right to Hawlucha on third-and-seven, with 3:23 remaining in the first quarter. That was already a warning about the matchup: Cinnabar could create a difficult down without ending the possession. Later in the quarter, Tatsugiri intercepted Hatterene’s deep throw left and returned it nine yards. The Blaze had a response, and it was substantial enough to keep the game balanced.

Seismitoad scored on an eight-yard run early in the second quarter. Blackthorn regained the lead with Cacturne’s forty-five-yard field goal; Cinnabar answered with Charjabug’s twenty-three-yarder five seconds before halftime. At 10–10, the opening interception and the Blaze’s ability to finish its short scoring opportunity gave the home team something real to build on. Anyone claiming the result was settled from the opening kickoff should explain that halftime score.

The third quarter supplied the explanation for everything that followed. Hatterene found Simeon Ice, the Glalie wearing number 97, for a twelve-yard touchdown at 4:35. Cinnabar then reached fourth-and-one and chose to keep its offense on the field. Vigoroth sacked Gholdengo for a four-yard loss at 3:49. Blackthorn had a fresh possession and a seven-point lead; within forty-five seconds, Hatterene hit Hawlucha for a six-yard touchdown on third-and-five.

That sequence is where I would begin Cinnabar’s review. The fourth-down attempt had a clear reward: retain the ball and keep a one-score game manageable. Its failure gave the Dragons another chance before the Blaze had demonstrated an answer to the opening touchdown. The sack was credited to Vigoroth. The public play log does not establish which individual blocker missed an assignment, so no one gets a fabricated culprit to make the criticism tidier.

body.alt: Grovyle #18. Grovyle caught all nine targets for 135 yards. Editorial receiving illustration.
body.caption: Grovyle caught all nine targets for 135 yards. Editorial receiving illustration.

body.text: Gholdengo then threw deep left and was intercepted by Meganium, who returned the ball eleven yards. Hatterene’s next touchdown, a seven-yard pass to Hawlucha, arrived at 1:13. The third quarter ended 31–10. Three touchdown possessions had turned a tied road playoff game into a commanding lead, and Blackthorn had required neither a productive conventional running attack nor a defensive score to do it.
The receivers gave Hatterene different answers

Hawlucha’s five catches produced eighty-four yards and three touchdowns. Simeon Ice caught ten of thirteen targets for eighty-six yards and two scores. Grovyle’s perfect nine-for-nine afternoon produced the most receiving yardage on either team. Those lines describe three different contributions: finishing drives, supplying frequent completions and moving the offense substantial distances. Cinnabar could not solve the passing game by treating one receiver as its entire problem.

Hatterene’s final touchdown went to Simeon Ice for seven yards with two minutes remaining. By then the result was secure, but the completion finished an afternoon in which the quarterback had recovered from an early interception without shrinking the offense. The Dragons attempted thirty-seven passes and recorded only nine rushing attempts, three of them Hatterene’s closing kneels. They finished with ten rushing yards. This was a passing victory, and the evidence does not require us to pretend otherwise.

There is also a caution for the next round in that imbalance. Blackthorn won so convincingly because Hatterene and the receivers repeatedly completed the work. A road game at Mt. Silver may ask them to do it against a different defense and under different pressure. Five touchdown passes earn attention; they do not guarantee five more. The Dragons nevertheless leave Cinnabar with a much stronger recent case than a generic fifth seed arriving simply to make the bracket look complete.
Cinnabar could not sustain an answer

Gholdengo completed twenty of forty-three passes for 207 yards, with no touchdown passes and one interception. Octillery caught six of fifteen targets for forty-two yards. Beautifly caught three of ten for twenty-six. Those two receivers accounted for twenty-five targets and nine completions. The Blaze kept returning to a passing game that was producing too many empty downs, and Blackthorn’s ten recorded passes swatted compounded the difficulty.

Seismitoad’s nine carries produced forty-eight yards and Cinnabar’s only touchdown. The team finished with fifty-three rushing yards on ten attempts. That production does not prove the Blaze could have run its way back from a three-touchdown deficit; the score eventually changed what was feasible. It does show that the first-half route to points involved a successful run, while the second-half chase asked Gholdengo to carry an increasingly difficult passing burden.

Blackthorn sacked him four times. Vigoroth supplied three, including the fourth-and-one stop and a later seven-yard loss during Cinnabar’s final extended possession. Leavanny added another. The Dragons’ defense did not need to win every snap. It needed enough disruptive ones to prevent Cinnabar from turning its 260 total yards into another touchdown. The Blaze finished with twelve first downs and ten points, both achieved before the game’s final separation had run its course.

body.alt: Glalie #97, Hawlucha #88. Simeon Ice and Hawlucha combined for five touchdown catches. Imagined postgame scene.
body.caption: Simeon Ice and Hawlucha combined for five touchdown catches. Imagined postgame scene.

body.text: The late possession illustrated the problem without explaining the whole afternoon. Cinnabar converted one fourth-and-seven on a completion to Thievul, took another sack, and eventually failed on fourth-and-one when Blastoise broke up a short pass intended for Gastly. There were individual completions worth keeping. There was no sustained scoring response. Blackthorn then used three kneels to finish a road playoff win that had become comfortable well before the final whistle.
The Dragons have earned the harder assignment

Both clubs entered the postseason at 12–5. Cinnabar had the division title and the home game; Blackthorn had lost the Johto East finale in Lavender on a last-second field goal. One week later, the Dragons are advancing and the Blaze are finished. That is enough reason to resist treating either seed or the most recent heartbreak as a complete description of a team.

I will take the loss on my Cinnabar pick. The Blaze offered a credible first half, and Blackthorn supplied the far better second one. A defense that gives up four touchdown passes after intermission cannot ask its reputation to fill the missing possessions. An offense with two third-down conversions in eleven attempts cannot make a convincing claim that the quarterback simply ran out of time.

Mt. Silver now gets Hatterene, Grovyle, Hawlucha and Simeon Ice with a conference-final place at stake. The Reds have their own season’s worth of evidence, their own injuries and a home field they earned. Blackthorn arrives with a specific challenge for them: cover several productive receivers, survive the quarterback’s willingness to keep throwing, and finish the difficult downs that Cinnabar repeatedly allowed to become new scoring opportunities.

articles.title: Hobbes gives Lavender seventy-three yards of breathing room
articles.dek: A late kickoff return sets up Moth Ball’s winning pass, and the Wails survive Vermilion 24–21 to reach Saffron.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Lavender had just allowed the touchdown that might have ended its season. Vermilion led 21–17 with fifty-three seconds left, and the Wails were about to receive a kickoff with a familiar obligation: make a very small amount of time sufficient. Hobbes caught the kick and returned it seventy-three yards to the Vermilion 22. Three passes later, Lavender led again.

Moth Ball found People Eater for sixteen yards, Samurott for five and Diggersby for the final yard. The touchdown arrived with thirty-six seconds remaining; Doc Ock’s extra point made it 24–21. Vermilion still reached a fifty-nine-yard field-goal attempt, but Shiinotic missed wide left with six seconds showing. The Wails advanced to Saffron, carrying a ninth consecutive victory and another ending that probably ought to come with a chair.

I am reluctant to call this a habit that can be safely maintained. Lavender had needed two late completions and a field goal to beat Blackthorn in the division finale. Here, it needed an enormous return before the offense could finish its rescue. Those are real achievements by real contributors. They are also a narrow way to keep a season alive, particularly with a 42-point Saffron team waiting in the divisional round.
The return changed the work required

The return gave us field position. The offense finished the possession. We also allowed nineteen first downs. All three things happened. We will prepare for Saffron by dealing with all three, because the last touchdown does not remove the work that came before it.
body.speaker: Travis Scarboro

body.text: Vermilion’s go-ahead possession was a strong one. Reuniclus converted fourth-and-two with a fifteen-yard pass to Galvantula at 1:41. He then kept moving the ball through short completions, including two to Camerupt. The second of those went eleven yards for a touchdown at 0:56. Shiinotic’s extra point put the Volts four points ahead, requiring Lavender to reach the end zone rather than settle for a tying kick.

Hobbes made that requirement much less distant. The Arcanine’s seventy-three-yard return placed the ball at the Vermilion 22 with enough time for the offense to operate immediately. Moth Ball did not need to string together a full-field possession or spend the first several plays escaping his own territory. His sixteen-yard pass to People Eater at 0:43 reduced the remaining distance to six yards. Samurott’s five-yard catch went out of bounds at 0:39.

Diggersby caught the one-yard touchdown pass short right at 0:36. He finished with two catches on two targets for four yards, a receiving line that would look modest anywhere except the part of the record that decides whether a club plays again. The Wails used three different receivers on the winning possession. Moth Ball’s final numbers were fifteen completions in twenty-six attempts, 148 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions.

That last point matters because Lavender could not afford to make its limited offensive production smaller. The Wails gained 218 total yards to Vermilion’s 368 and recorded nine first downs to the Volts’ nineteen. They ran forty-six plays to Vermilion’s sixty-three. They survived those differences through field position, timely scoring and four sacks. The return totals were particularly striking: Lavender gained 283 yards on eight returns, while Vermilion gained eighty-four on six.

body.alt: Frosmoth #15, Diggersby #43. Moth Ball found Diggersby for the one-yard winning touchdown. Illustration of the recorded play.
body.caption: Moth Ball found Diggersby for the one-yard winning touchdown. Illustration of the recorded play.

body.text: A long afternoon before the final minute

Doc Ock opened the scoring with a forty-three-yard field goal at 4:23 of the first quarter. Vermilion answered with Kangaskhan’s six-yard touchdown run to the right. The Volts led 7–3 at halftime after a second quarter with no scoring, although both quarterbacks had reason to remember the pass rush. Moth Ball took two first-quarter sacks; Reuniclus was sacked three times before the interval.

Lavender moved in front during the third quarter when Nidorina scored on a two-yard run up the middle. The Wails led 10–7 entering the fourth. Vermilion then regained the lead on a one-yard touchdown pass from Reuniclus to Ariados at 4:14. This was already a game in which possession of the lead felt provisional, but the actual sequence deserves more attention than the eventual reputation for drama.

Moth Ball responded with a twenty-two-yard touchdown pass short right to Cheep Caw at 2:43. The Unfezant finished with two catches for thirty-seven yards, and the score moved Lavender ahead 17–14 after the extra point. That possession gave the Wails a lead their defense still had to protect. Vermilion’s fourth-down conversion and Camerupt touchdown took it away, setting up Hobbes’s return and the final offensive reply.

The exchanges were not driven by a stream of turnovers. Neither team threw an interception or lost a fumble. Vermilion’s offense created its scoring opportunities through completions and a running game that gained 138 yards. Lavender answered with fewer total yards and much better return production. Reducing the result to one team being careless would miss the work the other actually performed.
Vermilion earned its chance to stay

Kangaskhan carried eighteen times for ninety-eight yards and a touchdown. Reuniclus completed twenty of thirty-five passes for 230 yards and two scores. Victreebel gained seventy receiving yards on three catches, including a fifty-one-yard reception. Camerupt caught six of seven targets for forty-two yards and the late touchdown. The Volts had enough offense to win a road playoff game, and for a brief stretch they were in position to do exactly that.

Their last possession began at their own 25 after a touchback. Kangaskhan gained eight yards, Galvantula caught a four-yard pass, and then Dugtrio sacked Reuniclus for a seven-yard loss with thirty seconds remaining. That sack was Dugtrio’s third of the game. It did not end Vermilion’s chance, but it lengthened the route to a manageable kick at the moment when time was becoming scarce.

After another short run, Reuniclus found Galvantula deep left for twenty-five yards at 0:18. Shiinotic attempted the fifty-nine-yarder at 0:06 and missed wide left. A kick from that distance is a consequential final act; it is a poor place to put the whole responsibility for an afternoon. The Volts had allowed the seventy-three-yard return that made Lavender’s answer possible and then surrendered three consecutive completions for the touchdown.

body.alt: Reuniclus #12. Vermilion’s final fifty-nine-yard field-goal attempt missed. Imagined sideline reaction by Reuniclus.
body.caption: Vermilion’s final fifty-nine-yard field-goal attempt missed. Imagined sideline reaction by Reuniclus.

body.text: Lavender’s defense contributed the sack that made the final drive harder. Blathers, the Rhyperior, supplied the other first-half sack alongside Dugtrio’s work. The published game record credits four sacks against Reuniclus, while Moth Ball took two. Those plays were especially valuable in a game where the Wails were otherwise allowing more first downs and more yardage than they created themselves.
Another trip for a team that keeps extending its season

Travis Scarboro will have plenty to review before Saffron. The Wails converted three of nine third downs and produced only 148 passing yards. Their opponent controlled more offensive volume and nearly won. Lavender can be pleased with Hobbes’s return, Moth Ball’s final three throws and the defense’s late sack while still treating the broader performance as something that needs improvement.

Hobbes also led the rushing attack with sixty-two yards on nine carries. That contribution helps explain why the returner belongs near the center of this account. His afternoon included ordinary offensive work and the extraordinary field-position change that rescued the final minute. The Wails did not ask a previously uninvolved player to supply a miracle; they received another important play from someone already helping keep the offense moving.

Saffron will ask different questions. Its passing game just produced 266 yards and three touchdowns against Olivine, while its defense added a touchdown of its own. Lavender must make enough stops to keep that offense from building a lead too large for one return to repair. The Wails also need longer stretches of useful offense so their next late possession, if one is required, begins with a manageable assignment.

For now, the record contains another earned escape. People Eater, Samurott and Diggersby completed the final passing sequence; Hobbes supplied the distance that made it possible; Dugtrio complicated Vermilion’s answer. Lavender’s ninth straight win belongs to all of them. The next one would carry the Wails into the conference championship game, and Saffron has given them a very clear picture of how much work that will require.

articles.title: Petalburg keeps the ball when Rustboro needs it back
articles.dek: Two fourth-quarter touchdowns, two successful two-point tries and six third-down conversions send the Pride through, 29–23.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Rustboro had a five-point lead with 2:29 remaining and an offense that had not punted all afternoon. Petalburg still had the ball to come, which turned out to be the more consequential possession. Iron Valiant led the Pride back into the end zone, Glalie completed a second successful two-point conversion, and the defense forced three straight incompletions on Rustboro’s next series. Petalburg won 29–23 and will visit Sunyshore.

I want to begin with the third downs because the late touchdown depends on them. Petalburg converted six of nine. Rustboro converted two of six. The Pride gained fewer total yards, 274 to 289, and did not force a turnover, yet they kept enough possessions alive to produce twenty-one fourth-quarter points. Their offense gave itself repeated opportunities to finish. Rustboro’s final meaningful drive lasted four snaps and ended on an incomplete fourth-and-nine pass.

The Stone’s running game was productive. My Way, Son gained seventy yards and scored on eleven carries; Philly Gabite added sixty-three on twelve. Shawn Watzon threw two touchdowns without an interception. Those facts make the defeat more difficult to explain with a simple bad-offense label. Rustboro had offensive answers. It needed one more sustained answer after Petalburg took the lead, and that was when the passing game stopped connecting.
The last touchdown required two difficult conversions

We needed the conversion before we could think about the touchdown. Glameow made that catch, then Magneton finished the next third down. We have to take the same care into the next game and make the earlier defensive possessions less difficult for ourselves.
body.speaker: Norman

body.text: My Way, Son’s five-yard touchdown run to the right put Rustboro ahead 23–18 at 2:29. The attempted two-point pass afterward failed, leaving Petalburg able to move ahead with a touchdown. Iron Valiant then worked through a possession that included a ten-yard completion to Venomoth, a nine-yard completion to Seviper and a short run by Whiscash. The Pride reached third-and-eight after an incompletion intended for Magneton.

At 1:26, Iron Valiant threw short right to Glameow for fourteen yards. That conversion brought Petalburg to the Rustboro 4. Two incompletions followed, first toward Glameow and then Vikavolt. On third-and-four, Iron Valiant found Magneton short left for the touchdown at 1:10. Glalie ran up the middle for the successful two-point try, and the Pride led 26–23 with 1:08 remaining.

Glameow finished with one catch for fourteen yards. Magneton finished with one catch for four yards. Both catches belonged to that final touchdown drive, and each answered a third down that could have left the Pride facing a much harder decision. A receiving leaderboard ordered by yardage would put them well below several teammates. The sequence explains why their contributions deserve prominent space in the game report.

Rustboro began its reply at its own 21 after Gengar’s seventeen-yard return. Philly Gabite gained one yard. Watzon then missed a short pass toward Gabite, had a deep throw toward Sudowoodo broken up by Rampardos, and missed Gengar on fourth-and-nine. Petalburg took over with fifty-five seconds left. Three Glalie runs used time and Rustboro’s remaining opportunities to stop it before Sunflora made a thirty-seven-yard field goal at 0:10.

body.alt: Glalie #95. Glalie converted the two-point try after Petalburg’s go-ahead touchdown. Editorial illustration.
body.caption: Glalie converted the two-point try after Petalburg’s go-ahead touchdown. Editorial illustration.

body.text: The final squib kick left Rustboro with four seconds. A one-yard run ended the afternoon. The decisive stop had already happened on the preceding possession, when the Pride defended three passes after allowing only one yard on first down. There was no late interception to decorate it. Petalburg simply denied the conversion that Rustboro needed to keep its season going.
A divisional game that stayed close

Iron Valiant opened the scoring with a one-yard touchdown pass to Seviper late in the first quarter. Rustboro answered almost immediately through its biggest passing play: Watzon found Gibby Timmy deep left for a forty-six-yard touchdown with six seconds left in the quarter. Both kickers made their first extra points. The teams traded field goals in the second quarter and entered halftime tied 10–10.

Petalburg’s Sunflora made a forty-eight-yarder at 3:21. Rustboro’s Gorebyss answered from thirty-nine yards at 0:52. The Pride’s Parasect had sacked Watzon for six yards during that Rustboro possession, the only sack recorded by either team. That pressure mattered without wrecking the entire drive; the Stone still came away with points. A close game often contains useful defensive plays that limit a possession rather than ending it outright.

Watzon found Geodude for a five-yard touchdown in the third quarter, moving Rustboro ahead 17–10 after the extra point. Petalburg replied early in the fourth with Glalie’s four-yard run up the middle. Iron Valiant then ran left for the two-point conversion, putting the Pride in front 18–17. My Way, Son’s touchdown restored Rustboro’s lead, setting up the final Petalburg scoring drive.

Those conversion decisions changed the score progression. Petalburg succeeded on both of its two-point tries and earned four points from them. Rustboro made its two conventional extra points and failed on the try following its third touchdown. The final margin was six, but the additional conversion points had already affected what each team needed on its subsequent possession. Petalburg’s second touchdown of the fourth quarter created a three-point lead rather than a one-point one.
Useful offense can still leave a team short

Watzon completed ten of sixteen passes for 126 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Gibby Timmy caught both of his targets for fifty-five yards; Geodude caught all four of his for thirty-three. Rustboro gained 163 rushing yards on twenty-seven carries and finished without a punt. The Stone also committed no recorded turnovers. This was a game lost despite several forms of offensive efficiency, which makes the defensive inability to finish third downs especially costly.

Petalburg’s quarterback completed seventeen of thirty for 141 yards and two touchdowns, adding thirty-nine rushing yards on five attempts. Glalie carried fourteen times for sixty-four yards and a score. Whiscash supplied thirty yards on five carries. The Pride generated seventeen first downs and ran fifty-four plays. They did not need a long touchdown to produce the winning drive; they needed several short completions, two difficult third-down answers and a final finish near the goal line.

body.text: Tyler Scarboro will have a specific defensive sequence to study rather than a general complaint about effort. Glameow gained fourteen on third-and-eight. Magneton scored on third-and-four after consecutive incompletions. Both plays came on the possession that changed the winner. The record does not reveal a private coverage call or assign blame to a particular defender, so the responsible diagnosis stops at the observed failure to secure those downs.

The same standard applies to Rustboro’s last possession. Three incompletions are enough to describe the result. They do not justify inventing a dropped pass, a missed read or a receiver running the wrong route. Rampardos’s breakup on the third-down throw is recorded and deserves credit. The other failures remain incomplete passes in the evidence available to readers.
Sunyshore will demand another complete finish

Petalburg entered the playoffs as a 12–5 division winner with a negative regular-season point differential. That combination invited skepticism, including fair questions about the Pride’s ability to score against strong opposition. Their wild-card win supplies a concrete response: twenty-nine points, a decisive fourth-quarter drive and a defensive stop when a rival needed one more possession. It does not erase the earlier season, but it earns the next game on its own terms.

Sunyshore just held Hearthome to six points and nineteen rushing yards. Petalburg will have to sustain its offense against a defense arriving with a much stronger recent performance than Rustboro’s third-down record. Oinkologne remains listed with one week of recovery, and Glalie’s new minor entry carries no remaining absence. Neither line should be turned into an invented lineup announcement. The Pride’s confirmed contributors have already shown what they can do in a close elimination game.

Rustboro finishes with a narrow defeat after a 9–8 regular season. Its running production and two clean touchdown throws made advancement possible; its inability to get the last needed stop, then the last needed conversion, decided the outcome. Petalburg travels on with the players who made those moments work. Glameow and Magneton will not lead the week’s yardage tables, but Sunyshore would be sensible to watch their third-down catches closely.

articles.title: Saffron turns a 10–7 deficit into thirty-five unanswered points
articles.dek: Archam Manning throws three touchdowns, Dam Skattebo runs for two, and Jack Slampert supplies the defensive finish in a 42–10 win.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Olivine led Saffron 10–7 in the second quarter. This is worth preserving because the final score, 42–10, is large enough to encourage everyone to misremember the first part. The Ironclads had intercepted Archam Manning and converted the resulting opportunity into a touchdown. Saffron then scored the next thirty-five points. The suspense lasted longer than the scoreboard now suggests, and substantially less long than Olivine needed.

Manning threw for 266 yards and three touchdowns. HeeDee Lamb caught six passes for 143 yards. Dam Skattebo ran for ninety-four yards and two scores. Jack Slampert returned an interception twenty yards for a touchdown. The Psi Corps advance to host Lavender, which has made late escapes a specialty and will now encounter a team that spent the second half making an escape unnecessary.

I have been accused of liking Saffron too much. I will allow the prosecution to use my previous columns. For this game, however, the evidence is unusually cooperative: 377 total yards to Olivine’s 181, three passing touchdowns, two rushing touchdowns and a second-half shutout. The most serious new concern is Emmitt Smoth’s five-week injury designation. Winning comfortably did not make the afternoon cost-free.
Olivine gave the favorite something to answer

Emmitt helped us get here, and we are going to miss having him available. The players who are healthy have a job to carry forward. I loved the response after we fell behind, and I want that same commitment in the preparation for Lavender.
body.speaker: Trent Scarboro

body.text: The Ironclads opened with a drive that ended in Sunflora’s forty-yard field goal at 3:37 of the first quarter. Mamoswine had begun that possession with an eighteen-yard run, and Drampa completed enough short passes to keep it moving despite a seven-yard sack by Chen Norton Jr. Olivine had three points and an early demonstration that it could reach scoring range.

Saffron replied with a fifty-two-yard touchdown drive. Manning found HeeDee Lamb for twenty-six yards deep left, then ten more on a short throw to the same side. Mothel Irving caught the three-yard touchdown pass short right at 2:09. The Psi Corps led 7–3. That opening answer used Lamb to move the offense and a different receiver to finish it, a pattern the Ironclads would struggle to contain throughout the game.

Manning’s first pass of the second quarter was intercepted by Olivine’s Ninetales and returned seventeen yards. The Ironclads used the resulting short field, with Bibarel scoring on a three-yard run up the middle at 4:08. Olivine led 10–7. It was a genuine opportunity for the seventh seed, earned through a defensive takeaway and a completed scoring possession.

The response came through two Saffron touchdown passes before halftime. Manning hit Lamb deep middle for twenty-two yards on third-and-four at 2:01. Later, facing third-and-two with ten seconds left, he found Bysson Witten short left for fourteen yards and another score. Saffron went to halftime ahead 21–10. The interception remained in Manning’s line, but it had not forced the offense into a cautious retreat.

body.alt: Heliolisk #11. HeeDee Lamb caught six passes for 143 yards. Editorial receiving illustration.
body.caption: HeeDee Lamb caught six passes for 143 yards. Editorial receiving illustration.

body.text: The third downs went to the passing game

Those two second-quarter touchdown throws were particularly damaging because Olivine had reached a down on which a stop would have changed the possession. Instead, Saffron scored from twenty-two and fourteen yards. The Psi Corps finished three of six on third down. Olivine finished three of twelve. The difference in conversion rate helped turn a brief underdog lead into a game with very few remaining possessions available for a comeback.

Manning completed seventeen of twenty-four attempts, with one interception and one sack taken. Lamb caught six of seven targets. Witten caught six of eight for sixty-three yards, and Mothel Irving added three catches for thirty-eight. Gengar Pickens supplied two catches for twenty-two yards. Saffron’s three touchdown passes went to three different receivers, preventing the Ironclads from reducing the scoring problem to one matchup.

Lamb’s longest catch gained forty-five yards, and his 143-yard total came on only six receptions. That production is why the headline receiving line belongs to him even though Witten matched his catch count. Both contributions mattered: one created large gains, the other repeatedly gave Manning a completion and finished the half with a touchdown. Their combined twelve catches accounted for most of the passing game’s successful attempts.

The new injury entries require a careful distinction. Lamb and Pach Tatum have minor entries with zero weeks remaining. Emmitt Smoth is listed for five weeks. The first two entries do not support an invented absence; the third is a substantial availability loss for the next round. Smoth had two carries for fourteen yards before the game ended, and the evidence does not timestamp the injury within a specific play.
Skattebo and Slampert close the game

Dam Skattebo scored on a fourteen-yard run up the middle at 4:18 of the third quarter. His second touchdown came on a ten-yard run to the right at 4:13 of the fourth. Those scores extended Saffron’s lead to 35–10. The Darmanitan finished with thirteen carries for ninety-four yards, averaging more than seven yards per attempt, and supplied the rushing work that allowed the offense to keep scoring after halftime.

Olivine’s following possession began with NeMarcus Tare sacking Drampa for six yards. On third-and-thirteen, Drampa’s short throw right was intercepted by Jack Slampert, who returned it twenty yards for a touchdown at 3:47. The score reached 42–10 after the extra point. Slampert finished with six tackles, the interception and the defensive touchdown, earning the game’s defensive-player honor.

That sequence put a defensive conclusion on an offensive win. Saffron had already established a comfortable lead, but the sack and interception prevented Olivine from using the remaining time to produce even a modest second-half response. Chen Norton Jr. added another seven-yard sack on the next Ironclads possession. He finished with two sacks; Tare had one. The pressure was productive without requiring a claim that every Olivine passing failure came from the same cause.

body.alt: Darmanitan #22. Dam Skattebo rushed for ninety-four yards and two touchdowns. Editorial rushing illustration.
body.caption: Dam Skattebo rushed for ninety-four yards and two touchdowns. Editorial rushing illustration.

body.text: Olivine’s final extended attempt ended on fourth-and-seven when Drampa completed a six-yard pass to Carnivine. Furfrou made the tackle. Saffron then ran twice with Skattebo and finished with Manning’s kneel. The final stop was one yard short of the conversion, an appropriately exact ending for a defense that had repeatedly made the Ironclads work through unhelpful down-and-distance situations.
Olivine’s season ends with a limited passing answer

Drampa completed fourteen of twenty-five passes for 118 yards, no touchdowns and one interception. Mamoswine led the rushing attack with sixty-six yards on eleven carries, but the rest of the ground production was much less effective. Olivine finished with sixty-three rushing yards overall after negative quarterback yardage and several short gains. Bibarel’s touchdown was valuable; his six carries produced six yards.

Delcatty led the receivers with forty-seven yards on three catches. Veluza added twenty-three, Mamoswine eighteen and Quilladin eleven. The Ironclads had one long Delcatty catch of thirty-four yards, but they did not produce enough sustained passing offense to keep pace after Saffron’s second-quarter answer. Nine first downs and four punts left them with a shrinking set of ways to recover the score.

Olivine entered as a 9–8 wild card and briefly led one of the conference’s strongest teams. That early work belongs in its account alongside the defeat. The full season review can wait for the offseason issue; this game ended because Saffron repeatedly scored touchdowns while the Ironclads stopped scoring altogether. No elaborate explanation is required to make a thirty-five-point unanswered run consequential.

Lavender now brings its return game, its late-possession nerve and its nine-game winning streak to Saffron. Trent Scarboro’s team has a clear advantage to build on: several different players just turned useful possessions into touchdowns. It also has a clear task after Smoth’s injury: preserve the backfield’s effectiveness with the healthy players actually available. Forty-two points make a persuasive opening statement. The divisional round will test whether Saffron can repeat the underlying execution against a survivor with a much better recent record.

articles.title: Sunyshore wins the ground game, then takes the fourth-down chance
articles.dek: Myles Gabite rushes for 106 yards, Kobra Khan catches two touchdowns, and the Starseekers hold Hearthome to six points.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Sunyshore’s most consequential throw came on fourth-and-five with eighteen seconds left in the first half. DeZhaun Watzon found Kobra Khan short left for a seventeen-yard touchdown, turning a 7–6 lead into a 13–6 halftime advantage. The Starseekers had backed their offense to finish the possession, and it did. They never allowed another Hearthome point, winning 23–6 to earn a divisional home game against Petalburg.

Myles Gabite supplied the game’s most consistent offensive work, carrying fifteen times for 106 yards and a touchdown. Sunyshore gained 143 rushing yards while holding Hearthome to nineteen. Watzon threw two touchdowns, both to Kobra Khan, and took no sacks. That combination gave the Starseekers several ways to maintain control even when their passing yardage was modest.

I picked Sunyshore, and the defensive part of the argument held up. Hearthome managed eight first downs and 175 total yards. Its one touchdown briefly made the game close in the second quarter, but the Haunts could not build a running game or sustain enough passing offense to keep threatening. The Starseekers did not need a spectacular quarterback line to advance. They needed useful completions, a productive ground attack and a defense that kept answering.
The fourth-down throw changed halftime

Myles gave us the kind of work you can build a whole afternoon around. The defense gave us time to keep doing it. We earned another home game, and now Petalburg gets our attention. The crowd can enjoy this one while we prepare for the next one.
body.speaker: Karson Jones

body.text: Myles Gabite opened the scoring with a two-yard run up the middle at 2:31 of the first quarter. Kayden Lyons made the extra point, giving Sunyshore a 7–0 lead. Hearthome replied in the second quarter when Frosmoth found Haunter deep left for a twenty-one-yard touchdown at 3:37. The missed extra point left the score 7–6, close enough for the next scoring opportunity to carry real weight.

Sunyshore’s late-half possession reached fourth-and-five. Watzon’s short-left throw to Kobra Khan went seventeen yards for the touchdown at 0:18. The extra point failed, but the Starseekers still took a seven-point lead into halftime. The decision to keep the offense on the field produced six points and made Hearthome’s otherwise competitive first half end with a more difficult second-half assignment.

Kobra Khan would score again in the fourth quarter on a short-right completion recorded in the play log as eighteen yards. The game’s receiving table credits him with two catches, thirty-four yards and two touchdowns, with a listed long of seventeen; the play descriptions and aggregate yardage differ by one yard. The touchdowns agree across both records. We retain the official table and recorded descriptions as supplied rather than inventing a correction.

The larger point is unaffected by that small reporting discrepancy. Both of the receiver’s catches ended in touchdowns. Fera LaGatr did the heavier receiving work between those moments, catching nine of ten targets for eighty-seven yards. Sunyshore had a frequent completion available and a separate receiver who finished its two passing scores. Watzon completed eighteen of thirty attempts for 164 yards without an interception.

body.alt: Arbok #19. Kobra Khan caught both of Sunyshore’s touchdown passes. Editorial receiving illustration.
body.caption: Kobra Khan caught both of Sunyshore’s touchdown passes. Editorial receiving illustration.

body.text: Gabite kept the offense in workable situations

The Garchomp wearing number 99 averaged just over seven yards per carry. His longest run gained seventeen yards, so the 106-yard total was built through repeated useful attempts rather than one enormous breakaway. BAXXED? added thirty-one yards on six carries. Watzon and Jolt Vick contributed short rushing gains as well, giving Sunyshore twenty-three carries for 143 yards.

That production mattered against an opponent whose own ground game could not stay productive. Gumshoos carried seven times for seven yards. Palafin gained nine on three attempts, and Litleo gained four on three. Hearthome finished with nineteen rushing yards on fourteen carries. Its longest individual run was six yards. The Haunts repeatedly needed their passing game to supply distance that Sunyshore could obtain on the ground.

Gabite’s last three runs also helped finish the game. After Hearthome’s late interception, he gained five yards up the middle, six to the right and twelve to the left. Those carries used the remaining time and secured the result without requiring another pass. The final sequence is a useful illustration of what the running game had provided throughout the afternoon: gains large enough to change the next down and reduce the number of chances Hearthome would receive.

Karson Jones has a straightforward strength to carry into the next round. Sunyshore can ask its passing game to make important plays without asking it to supply every productive yard. That does not make the rushing output automatic against Petalburg. It gives the Pride a concrete problem to prepare for after a wild-card game in which Rustboro ran for 163 yards against them.
Hearthome’s passing game needed more help

Frosmoth completed sixteen of twenty-three passes for 156 yards, one touchdown and one interception. Abomasnow caught six of seven targets for eighty yards; Castform added four catches for thirty-four. Haunter’s touchdown accounted for most of his twenty-three receiving yards. The completion rate was respectable, but the offense did not create enough first downs or explosive gains to offset its limited rushing production.

Sunyshore sacked Frosmoth three times. Vigoroth recorded two of them, including a seven-yard loss with 2:19 left in the fourth quarter. Anorith supplied the other, a third-and-seven sack in the third. Those plays helped interrupt the possessions Hearthome needed to keep the score manageable. The Starseekers’ own quarterback finished without a sack taken, a substantial difference in an afternoon with relatively few total passing yards.

The Haunts also left kicking points behind. Sunflora missed the extra point following Haunter’s touchdown and missed the team’s only field-goal attempt. Those misses do not account for a seventeen-point defeat, but they reduced the reward for the limited scoring opportunities Hearthome created. Sunyshore’s Lyons made a fifty-six-yard field goal at 0:51 of the third quarter, extending the lead to 16–6 despite his earlier missed extra point.

body.alt: Porygon-Z #30. DeZhaun Watzon threw two touchdowns without an interception. Imagined postgame portrait.
body.caption: DeZhaun Watzon threw two touchdowns without an interception. Imagined postgame portrait.

body.text: Kobra Khan’s second touchdown came at 2:28 of the fourth. Lyons made that extra point, and Sunyshore led 23–6. On the following Hearthome possession, the Vigoroth sack was followed by an interception: Frosmoth threw deep left on third-and-eleven, and Sunyshore’s number 12 Ampharos returned the ball seventeen yards. Gabite’s final three carries then closed the game.
Petalburg brings a different late-game test

Hearthome entered at 8–8–1 and reached the playoffs through a crowded wild-card race. Its visit to Sunyshore ended with one touchdown and no second-half points. The full season accounting belongs in the offseason issue. For this elimination game, the record shows a defense that could not fully contain Gabite and an offense that lacked enough rushing support to keep challenging after halftime.

Sunyshore entered at 13–4 and now has a postseason win to accompany its division title. The Starseekers produced sixteen first downs, converted five of ten third downs and punted only once. Their offense ran fifty-three plays to Hearthome’s forty. Those measures support the result without requiring a claim that every part of the performance was polished. Watzon still had twelve incompletions, and the kicking unit missed an extra point.

Petalburg arrives after converting six of nine third downs and scoring twenty-one fourth-quarter points against Rustboro. That is a different challenge from Hearthome’s afternoon. Sunyshore will need to finish possessions against a quarterback who just made two difficult third-down throws on a go-ahead drive. Its own rushing attack has an inviting recent comparison, but the Pride have already shown they can win despite allowing substantial ground production.

The availability report also carries forward. 88 Special remains listed for fifteen weeks, while Serp Gardener, Nair Jordan and BJ Vickers have new minor entries with no remaining absence. Those zero-week entries do not establish an injury-related missed start. Sunyshore can prepare from its confirmed healthy options while continuing to account for the ongoing absence. The team’s next step is a home divisional game, with a running back in productive form and a defense that just allowed six points.

articles.title: Watchog finishes the drives Eterna cannot
articles.dek: Two five-yard touchdown runs and a late interception send Dewford to Mossdeep with a 20–9 road win.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Watchog scored from five yards out in the first quarter, then did it again in the second. Eterna answered with field goals. That distinction lasted the whole afternoon: Dewford reached the end zone twice, the Thorns never did, and the Breakers won 20–9 to earn a divisional trip to undefeated Mossdeep. A game with nearly equal total yardage turned on what each offense could do when points became available.

Dewford gained 225 yards to Eterna’s 232. Both teams recorded twelve first downs and threw one interception. Neither lost a fumble. The Breakers nevertheless led 14–0 before Eterna scored, then used two fourth-quarter field goals and Carnivine’s late interception to protect the advantage. The Thorns’ defensive reputation remained visible in stretches. Their offense could not produce the touchdown required to give that defense a winning margin.

I tend to distrust conclusions built from one afternoon, particularly when the conclusion tries to erase eleven regular-season wins. Eterna’s 11–6 season contained enough useful football to earn a home playoff game. This game supplied a narrower verdict: against Dewford, the Thorns converted one of eight third downs and settled for three field goals. Their season ended before the offense could change that pattern.
Dewford recovered from the first mistake

Watchog finished the two chances near the goal line, and the defense kept making them kick. That gave us a game we could manage. Mossdeep is a different assignment, and the work starts with understanding what we will need to do better on the next trip.
body.speaker: Brawly

body.text: The Breakers’ opening passing possession included an interception. Frosmoth threw deep left on third-and-five at 4:24 of the first quarter, and Eterna’s Gliscor returned it nineteen yards. An early road turnover could have given the Thorns the kind of low-scoring lead they preferred. Eterna did not turn it into points, and Dewford subsequently found the first touchdown.

Watchog ran right for five yards at 0:47. The extra point made it 7–0. His second touchdown came on another five-yard run, this time left, at 2:58 of the second quarter. Dewford led 14–0 after the kick. Watchog finished with seven carries for twenty-seven yards and two touchdowns, a line that makes more sense when the scoring opportunities are kept attached to the modest yardage total.

Excadrill supplied the larger share of the rushing workload, carrying sixteen times for sixty-four yards. Meowscarada gained twenty-one on two attempts, while Kricketune added five on four. Dewford finished with thirty carries for 120 yards. The Breakers did not overwhelm Eterna with a succession of long runs; they used enough productive rushing work to reach two short touchdown opportunities and then completed both.

That approach also limited what Frosmoth had to supply after the interception. He completed eleven of sixteen attempts for 105 yards, no touchdowns and one pick. Machoke caught five of six targets for thirty-two yards. Swellow added twenty-eight on two catches, and Excadrill caught a twenty-yard pass. The quarterback’s afternoon was modest, but it did not need to resemble Hatterene’s five-touchdown performance elsewhere in the bracket.

body.alt: Excadrill #46. Excadrill carried sixteen times for sixty-four yards. Editorial rushing illustration.
body.caption: Excadrill carried sixteen times for sixty-four yards. Editorial rushing illustration.

body.text: Eterna’s kicker kept the game available

Vikavolt made a fifty-seven-yard field goal at 1:52 of the second quarter, putting Eterna on the board. He added a twenty-four-yarder three seconds before halftime. The Thorns went to the interval trailing 14–6, close enough that a touchdown and a successful two-point try could have tied the game. Their kicker had converted both opportunities, including the unusually long first attempt.

The next Eterna score was another field goal. Slowking was sacked for seven yards on third-and-three at 2:56 of the third quarter, and Vikavolt made the forty-one-yard attempt eighteen seconds later. Dewford’s lead was down to 14–9. The Thorns had scored on three possessions without reaching the end zone, which kept the game close while leaving the offense with the same unfinished task.

Dewford answered in the fourth quarter with a forty-seven-yard field goal at 5:22. The score became 17–9, requiring Eterna to produce a touchdown and two-point conversion merely to draw level. The Breakers’ kicker is now listed as Camerupt in the box score; the recorded play descriptions retain Numel, the form used in the game. The identity is consistent even though the later display name reflects progression.

That distinction is small compared with the competitive one. Both kickers were perfect on field goals: Dewford two for two, Eterna three for three. The Thorns could not ask their kicker to solve a touchdown deficit by missing fewer kicks. He had already made all of them. Their offense needed to reach the end zone, and the Breakers repeatedly prevented that final step.
The interception that protected the final minutes

Eterna began another fourth-quarter possession with Slowking taking a seven-yard sack from Infernape. The Thorns continued trying to move the ball, but at 2:20 Slowking’s deep throw left was intercepted by Carnivine and returned sixteen yards. Dewford had the ball, an eight-point lead and a chance to use the remaining time while moving toward a final field goal.

Excadrill gained six yards up the middle at the two-minute warning. Watchog then converted third-and-one with a three-yard run left. The Breakers continued running, and their kicker made a thirty-seven-yard field goal with thirty-four seconds remaining. The lead was 20–9. Eterna now needed two scores with only a brief possession available, and the practical comeback window had closed.

Slowking completed a fifteen-yard fourth-down pass to Cramorant near the end, but it came too late to change the score. He finished eleven of twenty-four for 148 yards, with no touchdowns, one interception and two sacks taken. Trevenant led the receivers with fifty-eight yards on four catches. Marowak added forty-seven on three. Eterna had individual completions that moved the ball; it could not connect enough of them into a touchdown drive.

body.alt: Slowking #12. Eterna finished without a touchdown. Imagined postgame scene with Slowking.
body.caption: Eterna finished without a touchdown. Imagined postgame scene with Slowking.

body.text: Whiscash carried sixteen times for sixty-six yards, and Dodrio added eighteen on three attempts. The Thorns’ eighty-four rushing yards were useful without being decisive. When the offense reached third down, it converted only once in eight tries. Dewford converted four of eleven. Neither rate suggests an effortless offensive afternoon, but the Breakers found enough extra possessions and enough finishing plays to make the difference.
Mossdeep is familiar, and the assignment is larger

Dewford’s next opponent won all seventeen regular-season games, yet the Breakers have a specific reason to approach the trip with more than generic underdog optimism. They lost 24–21 to Mossdeep in Week 4. That result shows they previously kept a meeting close. It does not establish that the same sequence will repeat months of development and several roster decisions later, but it gives the preview an actual competitive history.

The wild-card win also follows Dewford’s 35–29 victory at Rustboro in the regular-season finale. The Breakers have advanced through two different kinds of games: a high-scoring finale featuring a major return play, then a more restrained road playoff game decided by rushing touchdowns and defensive stops. Their next opponent will have to prepare for both the return threat and the offense’s willingness to keep working through a running game.

Mossdeep’s own late-season results came with confirmed coaching intent to rest starters and give younger players opportunities. The Eclipse’s divisional personnel should be judged from what is actually selected, rather than assumed from those finale lineups. Dewford, meanwhile, has a new minor entry for Dusclops with zero weeks remaining and no positive-week injury listed among its current players. That gives the Breakers a comparatively clean availability report entering the trip.

Eterna leaves with a defense that kept the game within reach and an offense that never supplied the necessary touchdown. Dewford leaves with Watchog’s two finishes, Excadrill’s workload, Carnivine’s interception and a place in the final eight. The next destination is Mossdeep, where the Breakers will need more than a reminder that they once came close. They have earned the opportunity to find out whether this version can complete the job.

art.alt: Watchog #56. Watchog scored two five-yard rushing touchdowns. Illustration of the opening scoring run.

articles.title: Petalburg’s third-down receivers deserve the scouting report
articles.dek: Glameow and Magneton combined for eighteen receiving yards. Their two catches decided which team stayed alive.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: I want Glameow and Magneton at the front of Sunyshore’s Petalburg preparation. Put the season leaders on the next page. On the first page, show third-and-eight with 1:26 left and third-and-four with 1:10 left. Those are the snaps on which the Pride’s season could have ended and instead became a trip to the divisional round.

Glameow caught a fourteen-yard pass from Iron Valiant on the first. Magneton caught the four-yard touchdown on the second. They finished with one catch apiece. The combined eighteen yards would barely register in a league week containing Hatterene’s 367 passing yards and HeeDee Lamb’s 143 receiving yards. The sequence gives those eighteen yards their value: one catch kept the winning drive alive; the other completed it.

Petalburg converted six of nine third downs against Rustboro. That is the central offensive success I would carry into the next round. The Pride did not need a spectacular passing total. Iron Valiant threw for 141 yards, and the offense gained 274 overall. It needed enough completions at the moments when an incompletion would force a different decision. On the final touchdown drive, it made both of the difficult ones.
Two stops still leave a third snap

After Glameow’s conversion, Petalburg had first-and-goal at the Rustboro 4. Iron Valiant missed Glameow on first down and Vikavolt on second. Rustboro had won two consecutive passing snaps. The Stone still needed a third successful defensive play, and Magneton’s short-left catch made those earlier incompletions irrelevant to the possession’s ultimate result.

This is where the defensive review needs specificity. We have the direction of the throw, the receiver, the distance and the outcome. We do not have a reliable public assignment of a missed coverage responsibility to one defender. I can criticize the failure to end the possession without inventing a player who supposedly ignored his job. Sunyshore’s preparation should be equally disciplined: defend the situation, study the available targets and finish the down.

The Pride’s willingness to use different receivers also makes simple name recognition insufficient. Seviper caught five passes, while Glameow and Magneton caught one each. A defense that assumes the next important throw must go to the most productive target can leave the actual scoring option available. That is an analytical concern arising from the distribution, not a claim about Rustboro’s private coverage call.
Petalburg still has a defensive problem

I am giving the Pride credit for their conversions without clearing the rest of their performance. Rustboro rushed for 163 yards. My Way, Son gained seventy and Philly Gabite sixty-three. Sunyshore’s Myles Gabite has just gained 106 against Hearthome. Norman’s team is advancing with a clear concern that the next opponent is particularly well equipped to test.

The Pride cannot assume that another successful final drive will repair every earlier rushing gain. Sunyshore allowed six points in its wild-card game and did not give up a sack or interception on offense. If the Starseekers sustain their rushing production while protecting the ball, Petalburg may receive fewer favorable opportunities than it had against Rustboro. The third-down offense is a strength to use, not permission to ignore first-down defense.

Oinkologne remains out with one week reported. Glalie’s sixty-four rushing yards and touchdown provide an observed answer from the available backfield, and his new minor entry carries zero remaining weeks. The Pride should continue from the players who actually performed, while recognizing how much of the regular-season rushing workload remains absent.

I have Sunyshore winning 24–20. That is a close forecast because Petalburg’s late execution was real and because the Pride have repeatedly made modest scoring totals sufficient. The home team’s rushing advantage is the reason I lean the other way. If Petalburg advances again, I expect its report to contain another small receiving line attached to a very large down. Sunyshore should make sure it knows all the names before that snap arrives.

articles.title: Lavender’s returner has become part of the ending
articles.dek: Hobbes’s seventy-three yards changed the task for everyone who followed him. The Wails should remember the earlier work, too.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Hobbes gave Moth Ball twenty-two yards to cover instead of most of a field. That is the simplest useful description of Lavender’s winning kickoff return, and it is also the part of the ending most easily lost once the touchdown pass becomes the replay everyone remembers. The Arcanine’s seventy-three yards made the final three completions possible on a very different timetable.

Vermilion had just gone ahead 21–17. Fifty-three seconds remained. Lavender needed a touchdown, and the Volts had reason to believe their own late drive had finally settled the game. Hobbes returned the kick to the Vermilion 22. People Eater caught sixteen yards, Samurott five and Diggersby one. Moth Ball’s winning touchdown pass came with thirty-six seconds left. The Wails had used three throws and remarkably little time because the return had already completed most of the distance.

I like accounts of football that leave room for the player whose contribution changes somebody else’s job. Hobbes did not throw the touchdown. He did not catch it. He made the offense’s assignment shorter, and the offense then performed it cleanly. That is a fuller account than choosing between the returner and the quarterback as if the game had offered only one meaningful participant.
The ordinary work came first

Hobbes also rushed for sixty-two yards on nine carries. Lavender gained only 218 offensive yards, so that production mattered before the final return. He was helping the Wails remain close enough for the late play to change the winner. An account that begins and ends with the seventy-three-yard burst would miss much of his afternoon.

The Wails gained 283 return yards on eight returns, compared with Vermilion’s eighty-four on six. That difference helps explain how Lavender could win despite being outgained by 150 offensive yards. It also suggests that opponents should treat field position as a central part of the matchup. A team can defend an offense reasonably well and still spend the game defending too little field.

Saffron has just held Olivine scoreless after halftime while scoring thirty-five unanswered points. That makes the return preparation more consequential, because the Psi Corps have the offensive production to force Lavender into a chase. The Wails need more ordinary first downs, but a strong return can still change the scale of the next possession. Both statements can be true without asking Hobbes to reproduce the same distance every week.
Nine wins contain several different explanations

Lavender’s streak includes a 51–10 win at Violet, a 21–20 division-clinching finish against Blackthorn and this 24–21 escape from Vermilion. Those are different games. The streak is meaningful because the Wails keep winning them, not because each ending proves an identical theory of toughness. The large win showed scoring capacity. The narrow wins showed specific players completing specific late assignments.

Travis Scarboro will presumably have less use for the romantic version than I do. His team allowed nineteen first downs while gaining nine. The opponent passed for 230 yards and rushed for 138. Those are concrete reasons to demand improvement, even after a victory. A coach can appreciate the return and still want the offense to create more of its own field position.

My new round pick is Lavender 27, Saffron 24. I am aware of the size of Saffron’s recent scoring totals and the difficulty of that prediction. I expect Moth Ball’s low-interception passing and Hobbes’s field-position contribution to keep the Wails close enough for another late possession. That is my judgment, and it will remain attached to my name if Manning and Lamb make it look optimistic.

The final return deserves to be remembered as more than a prelude. Hobbes gave three receivers and a quarterback a manageable route to a touchdown. They completed it. Dugtrio then supplied a late sack that complicated Vermilion’s attempt to tie. Lavender’s ending belongs to several players working in sequence, which is a good reason to keep the whole sequence in view when the next game asks them to do it again.

articles.title: Cinnabar’s passing game left its best case at halftime
articles.dek: My Blaze pick failed because the offense stopped finishing possessions. The numbers identify the problem more clearly than another speech about belief.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: I gave Cinnabar a chance to win this game, and I gave that chance a score prediction. The Blaze lost 38–10. Their final passing line was twenty completions in forty-three attempts, 207 yards, no touchdown passes and one interception. I can acknowledge the error in my pick while still insisting on a precise account of why the team lost.

At halftime the score was 10–10. Cinnabar had intercepted Hatterene, scored through Seismitoad and added a field goal. Blackthorn had a passing touchdown and a field goal of its own. The Blaze’s case remained plausible at that point. The second half ended 28–0 to the Dragons, and Cinnabar’s offense did not supply a single scoring response.

The third-down line is the first place to look: two conversions in eleven attempts. Blackthorn converted four of eight. An offense that keeps surrendering its possessions cannot ask the defense to hold an increasingly productive quarterback indefinitely. Hatterene’s receivers were finishing their work, and Cinnabar’s passing game was leaving too much incomplete.
Twenty-five targets, nine completions

Octillery received fifteen targets and caught six for forty-two yards. Beautifly received ten and caught three for twenty-six. Together that is twenty-five targets, nine catches and sixty-eight yards. Those numbers do not identify the private route call or assign each failure to the quarterback, receiver or protection. They establish that a large share of the passing offense produced too few completed gains.

Thievul caught five of seven targets for forty-nine yards. Archaludon caught both targets for forty-seven. Roselia caught both for thirty-eight. Those useful individual lines make the broader distribution more frustrating, but they do not prove that simply redirecting every pass would have reproduced the same efficiency. Coverage and game situation change with the target. The responsible criticism is that the actual passing choices did not produce enough first downs or touchdowns.

Gholdengo was also sacked four times. Vigoroth supplied three, including the fourth-and-one stop after Blackthorn’s opening third-quarter touchdown. That was a pivotal failure: the Blaze were down seven, kept the offense on the field and lost four yards. The Dragons scored again before Cinnabar had established any second-half response.
The defense had its own failure to explain

Cinnabar allowed five touchdown passes. Hawlucha caught three and Simeon Ice two, while Grovyle caught all nine targets for 135 yards. The Blaze did not lose because one receiver made a single spectacular play. They repeatedly allowed Blackthorn to complete different parts of the passing task, including conversions and scoring throws to several targets.

Hatterene threw an interception early and still finished twenty-eight of thirty-seven for 367 yards. That recovery deserves credit. The Dragons did not become passive after the takeaway, and the defense did not give Cinnabar a matching scoring opportunity later. The second half therefore became a comparison between one passing game repeatedly finishing and another repeatedly returning the ball without points.

Seismitoad’s forty-eight rushing yards on nine carries included Cinnabar’s only touchdown. I am not going to manufacture a claim that nine more carries would have solved a twenty-one-point deficit. The score changed what the offense could reasonably pursue. The first-half rushing success remains part of the record; it does not erase the passing failure that defined the second half.

Cinnabar’s 12–5 division title remains earned. The broader season review and offseason decisions belong after the Indigo Bowl, when we can assess the whole year without using a playoff defeat as an excuse to rewrite every previous result. This week’s task is smaller and sharper: explain a home elimination game that was tied at halftime and then stopped being competitive.

I chose the Blaze because I believed their recent form and home defense could make Blackthorn’s passing offense uncomfortable for long enough. They managed one half of that argument. Hatterene completed the other half in the end zone four times. Cinnabar can preserve the division title, examine the failed passing possessions and prepare for the offseason. My old pick will remain in the archive with the score that disproved it.

articles.title: Mossdeep’s perfect season resumes against the team that came within three
articles.dek: Dewford returns with four straight wins, a healthy core and a 24–21 memory. The Eclipse begin the postseason with a much larger season-long case.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Dewford does not have to invent a reason to believe it can stay close to Mossdeep. The Breakers lost their Week 4 meeting 24–21, one of the few afternoons on which the Eclipse’s eventual perfect regular season looked seriously contested. Now they meet again, in Mossdeep, with a conference-final place available. The old score gives Dewford a starting point. The intervening season explains why the assignment remains so large.

Mossdeep finished 17–0, scoring 724 points and allowing 130. Dewford finished 11–6, then won 20–9 at Eterna in the wild-card round. The Breakers have won four straight, including a 35–29 finale victory at Rustboro. They have recently won with different kinds of production: a high-scoring road finish with a major return contribution, then a playoff game built around two short rushing touchdowns and a defense that never allowed the opponent into the end zone.

Michael Dorrill’s team has been waiting through the bye after a deliberate late-season rest policy. The coach confirmed that he was reducing starter injury exposure and giving younger players experience. That context belongs beside the Eclipse’s 22–3 win over Sootopolis and 27–0 shutout at Lavaridge. Those games cannot simply be treated as full-strength offensive auditions, and the divisional lineup should be confirmed from the actual selections rather than presumed from the finale.
The first meeting provides history, not a script

We rested players because we wanted them ready for this work. That does not buy anybody an excuse for a missed assignment. Dewford already showed us it can stay in a game with us. We need to execute the next play correctly, then do it again.
body.speaker: Michael Dorrill

body.text: The 24–21 result matters because it is an actual competitive meeting between these clubs. It does not tell us which later roster choices will be made or how the same players will perform after further development. Dewford’s useful lesson is that Mossdeep has already had to finish a close game against this opponent. Mossdeep’s useful lesson is equally concrete: the Breakers can create enough offense and field position to punish a careless afternoon.

The Eclipse’s season after that meeting provides a substantial counterweight. They beat Saffron 20–17, Rustboro 35–7, Petalburg 55–0 and Sunyshore 27–3. Their regular-season scoring margin reached plus-594. Those results establish a much broader performance record than the single close game in Dewford. The favorite’s case is built from repeated scoring and prevention, with the Week 4 score identifying a matchup worth taking seriously inside that record.

For Dorrill, the practical task is to restore the intended playoff roles without allowing the rest period to become an excuse for imprecision. His established standard leaves little room to celebrate ordinary competence as a special postseason achievement. The Eclipse earned home field so they could use it; their first elimination game still begins 0–0. A missed assignment will carry the same consequence whether it follows seventeen wins or a losing season.
Dewford must avoid a passing chase

Frosmoth completed eleven of sixteen passes for 105 yards against Eterna, with one interception and no touchdown passes. That was enough because Watchog scored twice on the ground and the defense held the Thorns to three field goals. A similar passing total could become much harder to live with if Mossdeep reaches twenty-one points early. Dewford needs its first several possessions to create useful field position and manageable downs, even when they do not immediately score.

Excadrill carried sixteen times for sixty-four yards in the wild-card win. Watchog added twenty-seven yards on seven carries, including the two five-yard touchdowns. Meowscarada contributed twenty-one yards on two rushes. Those roles gave the Breakers several ways to gain short and intermediate distances. Their challenge is to preserve that usefulness against a defense that allowed only 130 regular-season points, rather than asking Frosmoth to recover repeated long-yardage situations.

The quarterback’s regular season included 2,459 passing yards, twenty-six touchdowns and twelve interceptions. That line supports a credible passing contribution, but it also explains why possession security belongs near the top of Brawly’s preparation. An early interception at Eterna did not become an opposing touchdown. Mossdeep’s offensive production makes the same mistake potentially more expensive. Dewford cannot assume that another defensive rescue will keep the score unchanged.

Meowscarada’s return threat also deserves specific attention. The Breakers’ finale included a ninety-nine-yard kickoff-return touchdown against Rustboro. Mossdeep must prepare for field-position damage even on possessions where its defense has not yet taken the field. That is a checkable special-teams concern, not a forecast that the returner will repeat the play. Dewford’s strongest upset route includes making the Eclipse defend shorter fields than their season averages would ordinarily suggest.
Mossdeep has several established touchdown sources

Dram Marino finished the regular season with 4,341 passing yards, fifty-six touchdown passes and four interceptions. Accel BeckhmJr caught thirty-two touchdowns while gaining 1,953 receiving yards. Ninjaskamara rushed for 1,138 yards and twenty touchdowns. Gronkaludon contributed 830 receiving yards and nine scores, while Ninjulio Jones added 770 and seven. The volume is spread across enough roles to make a single-defender solution implausible.

Those are completed regular-season totals, separate from the postseason box scores. They also describe what the principal scorers have already done, rather than announcing the exact divisional depth chart. If the Eclipse return their main passing and rushing contributors to their expected work, Dewford has to defend several kinds of scoring pressure simultaneously. The Breakers cannot spend the entire game preventing one long reception while conceding every short rushing opportunity.

The Eterna result offers Dewford a useful defensive model at the level of outcomes: limit touchdowns, force difficult third downs and finish the late takeaway. The Breakers held the Thorns to one conversion in eight third-down attempts and intercepted Slowking with 2:20 left. Reproducing those outcomes against Marino is a much harder assignment. His four regular-season interceptions came alongside fifty-six touchdown passes, leaving opponents very little evidence of routine giveaways to rely on.

For Mossdeep, the offensive key is to turn its stronger production into actual touchdown possessions before the game becomes a return-and-field-goal contest. The 24–21 first meeting gives the home team no reason to be casual about missed opportunities. Dewford has just demonstrated that it can win a road elimination game with 225 total yards. The Eclipse should make the Breakers exceed that offensive demand rather than voluntarily leaving them a low target.
Availability and the final possession

Poury Holt remains listed with five weeks of recovery. His absence is confirmed; a specific replacement workload should come from the chosen lineup. Shawn Mareman’s earlier minor entry has cleared, and Richard Furman’s healthy designation does not by itself establish activation from injured reserve. Readers should distinguish a player being free of a recovery counter from a confirmed roster move or starting assignment.

Dewford has no positive-week injury among its current players in this export. Dusclops has a new minor entry with zero weeks remaining. That is a comparatively favorable report for a road team preparing to face a deeper scoring offense. It allows the Breakers to build around their available contributors without an additional confirmed absence from the wild-card game. It does not guarantee that every player will take the same role or workload again.

The winner will face either Sunyshore or Petalburg for the Hoenn–Sinnoh championship. Mossdeep would host that game as the top seed. Dewford, the fifth seed, would travel to either surviving division winner. Those paths explain the stakes without turning the divisional game into a preliminary formality. Both teams must earn the next fixture before its location matters.

My forecast is Mossdeep 35, Dewford 17. I expect the Breakers to create some offense through rushing and field position, with the earlier close meeting keeping the favorite attentive. The Eclipse’s passing efficiency and multiple established touchdown sources give them the stronger route to sustained scoring. Dewford’s upset requires the game to remain manageable long enough for its late-possession strengths to matter; Mossdeep’s task is to make that window smaller from the opening quarter.
