articles.title: Blackthorn returns to Mt. Silver with a passing game the Reds have already met
articles.dek: The Dragons won 30–22 here in Week 12. Hatterene’s five-touchdown opener raises the stakes for an injured top seed coming off its bye.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Blackthorn’s trip to Mt. Silver is a return visit to a place where the Dragons have already won. Their 30–22 victory in Week 12 gives this divisional game a specific history, and their 38–10 wild-card win at Cinnabar gives it immediate force. Hatterene arrives after five touchdown passes. The Reds arrive rested, at home and still dealing with several injuries that the bye did not fully resolve.

Mt. Silver earned the conference’s top seed with a 14–3 regular season, 481 points scored and 206 allowed. Blackthorn finished 12–5, scoring 385 and allowing 348. Those full-season records favor the Reds. The current matchup is less comfortable for them: Tic Thorpe still has two weeks reported, Josh Alakazam three, Tony Gyarzalez four, and Vibrava four. The top seed has a substantial season behind it and a narrower available group in front of it.

Garshawn Lynch is central to the home team’s answer. He led the league with 1,200 regular-season rushing yards, scored eleven rushing touchdowns and added four receiving scores. Blackthorn’s quarterback just won through repeated completions to several receivers. Mt. Silver’s clearest route is to sustain its own possessions, finish them and keep Hatterene from receiving a succession of extra opportunities against a defense forced back onto the field.
Hatterene has answered one difficult ending

Blackthorn has already won a game here, so I doubt they need help finding the entrance. We have earned the chance to give them a different afternoon. Garshawn has been giving people something to tackle all season. We will need the passing game to do its share, too, because Hatterene is unlikely to spend the day admiring our regular-season record.
body.speaker: Connor McLarren

body.text: The Dragons lost the Johto East finale 21–20 at Lavender on a last-second field goal. That defeat cost them the division and sent them to Cinnabar. They then entered halftime of the wild-card game tied 10–10 before scoring twenty-eight unanswered points. The response matters because it was observed: an early interception and a tied road game did not stop Hatterene from producing four second-half touchdown passes.

He completed twenty-eight of thirty-seven attempts for 367 yards. Grovyle caught all nine targets for 135 yards, Hawlucha caught three touchdowns and Simeon Ice caught two. The Dragons gained only ten rushing yards, with three closing kneels included in the total. Their win was carried by the passing game, supported by a defense that repeatedly stopped Cinnabar on third down and sacked Gholdengo four times.

That performance gives Mt. Silver several receiving problems to solve. Concentrating exclusively on the touchdown scorers would overlook Grovyle’s nine completions. Concentrating exclusively on yardage would overlook Hawlucha and Simeon Ice finishing drives. The Reds need to defend the full passing sequence: the early completion that creates a manageable down, the conversion that keeps a possession alive and the final throw near the end zone.

Hatterene’s regular-season totals reinforce the threat: 4,532 passing yards, thirty-eight touchdowns and eight interceptions. The wild-card line was an exceptional afternoon within an already substantial passing season. It should not be treated as a guaranteed repeat, especially against a stronger season-long defense. It does establish that Blackthorn can enter this rematch with a current offensive identity more specific than merely being a dangerous lower seed.
The Reds have a rushing answer and a quarterback question

Lynch’s production is the first reason to resist making the Dragons an automatic road choice. A runner who gained 1,200 yards can give the available quarterback shorter downs and can make Blackthorn defend stretches of offense rather than spend the afternoon preparing its next passing series. The Reds also beat Saffron 36–33 in Week 15. Their season includes a win over a contender capable of scoring at a much faster pace than Cinnabar managed in the wild-card round.

The recent results also include a 38–24 loss at Cinnabar and a 21–13 finale defeat against Cianwood. Those games should be read with the available personnel in mind, but the injury context does not erase the points conceded or the offensive limitations. Mt. Silver has to produce a working divisional plan from the players actually available. Its top seed does not restore an injured passer or a missing receiving target.

Crem Ftzpatrik completed the regular season with 1,004 passing yards, eight touchdowns and six interceptions. Tic Thorpe’s earlier work produced 1,560 yards, seventeen touchdowns and two interceptions, while Josh Alakazam and Jacoby Brizzet also contributed at quarterback. Those totals show a season divided among several passers. The preview should not quietly combine them into the performance of one healthy incumbent.

Tony Gyarzalez’s continuing absence removes a receiver who gained 948 yards and scored seven touchdowns during the regular season. Gregar Jenings produced 795 yards and six scores, Scep Smith Jr. added 633 and five, and Plusico Buress had 572 and four. There are remaining targets with recorded production. The question is whether the available quarterback and protection can connect with them often enough to keep pace with Hatterene.
A bye changes recovery, not every designation

Ninji Asomugha’s counter has reached zero after previously showing one week. That is a meaningful availability change, although it does not establish a particular starting assignment. Other absences remain positive: Ariados is listed for nine weeks and Medicham for three, alongside the quarterback, tight-end and backfield injuries. The Reds received a week without a game; they did not receive a fully cleared injury list.

Blackthorn’s Sawsbuck remains listed for three weeks. Exploud’s counter has reached zero after showing one. The returning designation could expand available options, but readers should wait for an actual role before assigning him a projected workload. The Dragons’ wild-card receiving distribution already gives us a confirmed account of how they functioned without assuming that every newly cleared player immediately resumed an old job.

This is why I prefer to frame the game around demands rather than a guessed formation. Blackthorn needs efficient passing and enough protection for Hatterene to use several receivers. Mt. Silver needs productive Lynch possessions and a passing contribution that does not give those possessions back through mistakes. Neither statement requires access to a private playbook, and both can be checked against the recorded game afterward.
The previous meeting makes the upset credible

The Week 12 result was Blackthorn 30, Mt. Silver 22 at the same home venue. It is evidence that the Dragons have already won this matchup on the road. It is not evidence that every matchup detail remains unchanged. Injuries, development and available roles have moved since then, and the divisional pressure changes the consequence of the result even when the field is familiar.

Mt. Silver’s strongest response would be to make the game feel different through its own offensive consistency. Lynch can reduce the frequency of long-yardage passing situations, while the remaining receivers can punish a defense that becomes too focused on the run. A home lead would allow the Reds to use that balance. An early two-score deficit would increase the burden on a quarterback group already missing important contributors.

Blackthorn’s defense has a recent success to carry forward: Cinnabar converted only two of eleven third downs and never scored after halftime. Vigoroth’s three sacks included a fourth-and-one stop that helped accelerate the third-quarter separation. The Reds will present a different rushing challenge from the Blaze, so those outcomes cannot simply be transferred. They do identify the kind of possession-ending plays that would make Hatterene’s task easier.

My forecast is Blackthorn 30, Mt. Silver 27. The Reds’ home field, rushing production and full-season defense keep this close. The Dragons have the clearer current passing performance and a prior win in the same matchup, while Mt. Silver’s continuing quarterback and tight-end absences make a late passing exchange harder. The winner reaches the Kanto–Johto championship game against Saffron or Lavender; Blackthorn would travel again, while a Mt. Silver win would preserve home field.

articles.title: Lavender takes nine straight wins into Saffron’s highest-pressure test
articles.dek: The Wails keep surviving late. The Psi Corps keep scoring early enough to make late drama optional. Their first meeting decides a conference finalist.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Lavender has won nine consecutive games and still arrives in Saffron as the team with more to explain. The Wails needed a last-second field goal to win their division, then a seventy-three-yard kickoff return to set up the touchdown that beat Vermilion. Saffron’s last four scores are seventy, thirty-one, forty-nine and forty-two. The meeting asks whether Lavender can bring the game down to a scale its late-possession strengths can manage.

There is no earlier meeting between these clubs in the season’s recorded schedule. Their arguments come from separate bodies of work. Saffron finished 14–3 with 597 points scored and 138 allowed. Lavender finished 12–5 with 325 scored and 317 allowed, then won its wild-card game 24–21. The Wails’ recent streak deserves real weight; the Psi Corps’ season-long scoring and defensive advantages deserve it too.

Travis Scarboro and Trent Scarboro bring distinct coaching temperaments to the same practical problem: win one game to reach the Kanto–Johto championship. Lavender’s coach has a long list of details to tighten after allowing 368 yards to Vermilion. Saffron’s coach has a new backfield absence to manage after Emmitt Smoth’s five-week injury. Neither can simply ask the latest winning score to settle the next matchup.
Lavender needs a more ordinary source of distance

The complete staff panel includes one Lavender pick and four Saffron picks. The disagreement concerns how much field position and late execution can narrow the larger offensive gap; all five forecasts remain editorial judgments rather than calibrated probabilities.

Hobbes’s return was the central change in the wild-card finish. Vermilion had taken a 21–17 lead with fifty-three seconds left. The Arcanine returned the kickoff seventy-three yards to the Volts’ 22, and Moth Ball completed three consecutive passes for the winning touchdown. The final sequence was excellent. It also began with a field-position gift so large that it would be unreasonable to build a whole divisional plan around receiving another one.

The Wails gained only 218 offensive yards and nine first downs against Vermilion. Moth Ball completed fifteen of twenty-six passes for 148 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Hobbes rushed for sixty-two yards on nine carries. Those contributions were enough because the return game supplied 283 yards on eight returns and the defense produced four sacks. Against Saffron, Lavender needs more first downs and more sustained offense before the final minute.

Moth Ball’s regular-season passing line offers one reason to believe in a controlled approach: twelve touchdown passes and one interception in 1,406 yards. His wild-card game also ended without an interception. Those numbers do not promise perfect possession security against Saffron’s defense. They do show a quarterback who has recently helped his team by avoiding the turnovers that could make a narrow game impossible to recover.

The receiver distribution in the final drive also matters. People Eater gained sixteen yards, Samurott five and Diggersby the last one. Lavender did not depend on a single target to make all three plays. The next challenge is to find that same sequence of useful completions over longer fields and earlier in the game, when a failed possession can still change the entire scoring pace rather than merely determine the last winner.
Saffron can score through several roles

Archam Manning led the regular season with 4,633 passing yards and threw forty-three touchdowns. HeeDee Lamb gained 1,878 receiving yards and scored eighteen receiving touchdowns. Dam Skattebo rushed for 1,026 yards and eighteen touchdowns. Those totals explain why Saffron can enter this game expecting more than one route to points, and the wild-card performance supplied a current example of all three contributors succeeding together.

Manning completed seventeen of twenty-four passes for 266 yards and three touchdowns against Olivine. Lamb caught six passes for 143 yards. Skattebo ran for ninety-four yards and two scores. Bysson Witten and Mothel Irving caught the other touchdown passes, and Jack Slampert added a twenty-yard interception return for a score. Olivine led 10–7 before Saffron produced thirty-five unanswered points.

The second-quarter touchdown throws are the most useful specific plays for Lavender to study. Manning found Lamb for twenty-two yards on third-and-four, then Witten for fourteen yards on third-and-two shortly before halftime. Those were opportunities for the defense to end possessions or force a different scoring choice. Saffron turned both into touchdowns. The Wails must finish those downs more often than Olivine did.

Lavender’s four sacks against Vermilion offer a possible response. Dugtrio had three, including the late sack that made the Volts’ final field-goal attempt harder. Blathers added another. The Wails will need pressure that changes Manning’s options without allowing the short completion to become another easy conversion. The recorded game does not reveal which private call will create that result; the preview can identify the required outcome without pretending to know the playbook.
Smoth’s absence changes the backfield calculation

Emmitt Smoth is listed for five weeks after the Olivine game. He carried twice for fourteen yards in that game, while Skattebo handled thirteen carries. The absence is meaningful because it removes an available contributor and narrows the backfield choices. It does not justify declaring that Saffron has lost its principal rushing production: Skattebo’s 1,026-yard regular season and ninety-four-yard wild-card performance remain the larger confirmed workload.

HeeDee Lamb and Pach Tatum have new minor entries with zero weeks remaining. Those should not be converted into questionable or doubtful labels that the game does not provide. They are distinct from Smoth’s positive recovery counter. Lavender’s Mr. Clanky remains listed for four weeks; Vikavolt and Axew have new minor entries with no remaining absence. The actual lineup will determine how the healthy options are used.

Availability therefore favors a practical comparison of the jobs already observed. Saffron needs to preserve rushing efficiency around Skattebo and maintain its several receiving threats. Lavender needs enough reliable offense from Moth Ball, Hobbes and the available receivers to avoid spending the afternoon chasing a rapidly growing total. Neither team should count an injured player’s earlier production as if it were automatically present in this game.

The coaching challenge is also different for the two clubs. Trent Scarboro can ask his team to repeat much of the execution that produced forty-two points, while adjusting the available backfield. Travis Scarboro needs to preserve the late composure and return value while improving the ordinary offensive possessions that preceded them. A nine-game streak supplies confidence; the 218-yard wild-card offense supplies specific work.
A return can change the game, but it cannot be scheduled

Saffron must treat Hobbes as part of its defensive preparation even when its defense is standing on the sideline. His return moved Lavender directly into touchdown range at the decisive moment. The Psi Corps can dominate several offensive comparisons and still make the game close if they repeatedly surrender short fields. Return coverage is therefore one of the preview’s clearest checks: make the Wails earn the distance with their offense.

Lavender’s route to an upset is equally concrete. Keep Manning from converting difficult downs into touchdowns, protect the ball, create useful return position and arrive at the fourth quarter within one possession. Ellis Quill has picked the Wails to win 27–24 on that basis. His forecast is a judgment about those strengths surviving a harder opponent, not a claim that late-game nerve overrides the rest of the matchup.

My forecast is Saffron 34, Lavender 21. I expect the Wails to create enough field-position value and short passing production to score, but Saffron has the stronger evidence for sustained touchdown drives. Manning’s receiving options and Skattebo’s rushing work should make the home offense less dependent on one decisive play. Smoth’s absence reduces flexibility without removing the main scoring contributors.

The winner faces Mt. Silver or Blackthorn. Saffron or Lavender would travel if the top-seeded Reds advance; either would host the fifth-seeded Dragons. The bracket therefore gives both teams a possible home conference championship, but only after this game is won. Lavender has extended its season nine times in succession. Saffron is preparing to make the tenth require substantially more than another final-minute escape.

articles.title: Petalburg brings its third-down finish to Sunyshore
articles.dek: The Pride survived 163 rushing yards against Rustboro. Myles Gabite and the Starseekers now ask whether they can do it again on the road.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Petalburg’s winning drive against Rustboro required fourteen yards on third-and-eight and four yards on third-and-four. Iron Valiant completed both throws, the second for a touchdown, and the Pride advanced 29–23. Sunyshore’s wild-card win offered a different kind of confidence: Myles Gabite rushed for 106 yards, Hearthome managed nineteen on the ground, and the Starseekers won 23–6. The divisional matchup brings those two forms of success together for the first time this season.

There is no recorded regular-season meeting between the clubs. Sunyshore finished 13–4, scoring 423 points and allowing 211. Petalburg finished 12–5, scoring 286 and allowing 292. Both won divisions. The Starseekers have the stronger season-long margin and home field, while the Pride have just demonstrated how a team with modest aggregate scoring can still execute the possessions that decide an elimination game.

Karson Jones’s team has a direct offensive target in the recent evidence. Rustboro gained 163 rushing yards against Petalburg, and Sunyshore’s own ground game just produced 143. That comparison does not guarantee another productive afternoon for Gabite. It does identify a matchup the Pride must improve if they want Iron Valiant’s late-drive composure to matter again.
Petalburg’s conversions are a real strength to respect

All five panelists favor Sunyshore, with projected margins ranging from two points to seventeen. That agreement on the winner contains a meaningful disagreement about how much Petalburg’s recent third-down execution will survive the change of opponent.

The Pride converted six of nine third downs against Rustboro. Their final touchdown drive included Glameow’s fourteen-yard catch on third-and-eight and Magneton’s four-yard score on third-and-four. Both receivers had only one catch, making the timing of those contributions more important than their place in the yardage rankings. Sunyshore must defend the available receiver on the decisive down rather than only the player with the largest season total.

Iron Valiant finished seventeen of thirty for 141 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions, adding thirty-nine rushing yards. Glalie carried fourteen times for sixty-four yards and a touchdown, then converted the second of Petalburg’s two successful two-point tries. Whiscash added thirty rushing yards. The offense created seventeen first downs without a long passing touchdown, and its twenty-one-point fourth quarter changed a close game into an advance.

The quarterback’s regular season included 2,556 passing yards, twenty-four touchdowns and ten interceptions. Seviper was a substantial established target, with 544 receiving yards and four touchdowns. Those totals provide useful context for the recent drive: Petalburg has a functioning passing offense, even if it does not approach the volume of Mossdeep or Saffron. The Pride need it to keep producing completions in situations where the defense knows a pass is plausible.

Sunyshore’s task is to reduce the number of second chances. Petalburg threw two incompletions from the Rustboro 4 before completing the winning touchdown. A defense can win two snaps in a row and still lose the possession if the third leaves the receiver available. The Starseekers’ recent six-point allowance is encouraging, but the game will be decided by whether they can finish those sequences against Iron Valiant.
Gabite gives Sunyshore a sustained source of yards

Myles Gabite carried fifteen times for 106 yards and a touchdown against Hearthome. His longest run was seventeen yards, so the production came from repeated gains rather than a single breakaway. BAXXED? added thirty-one yards on six attempts. Sunyshore gained sixteen first downs and ran fifty-three plays, allowing its passing game to contribute without carrying the entire offense.

Gabite’s closing sequence was particularly useful: five yards, six yards and twelve yards after Hearthome’s late interception. Those runs ended the game without another pass. Petalburg will want to prevent that kind of finish by keeping the score and the down-and-distance demands less comfortable. If the Starseekers can repeatedly run for a first down before the passing game faces pressure, the Pride’s defense will have fewer chances to create a possession-changing stop.

The Rustboro result shows both the concern and the caution in this comparison. Petalburg allowed substantial rushing production and still won. My Way, Son and Philly Gabite combined for 133 yards, yet the Pride made the last decisive stop through pass defense. Sunyshore should attack the apparent rushing opportunity while recognizing that yardage alone does not settle the game. It still has to turn drives into points and respond when Petalburg scores.

For Jones, that balance fits the wild-card performance. His offense produced three touchdowns: one on the ground and two through the air. The quarterback took no sacks and threw no interceptions. A similar level of possession security would make Petalburg earn its opportunities over full fields, reducing the chance that one successful late drive can erase an afternoon of superior movement.
Watzon’s targets must finish the important throws

DeZhaun Watzon completed eighteen of thirty passes for 164 yards against Hearthome. Fera LaGatr caught nine of ten targets for eighty-seven yards, providing the largest share of the receiving work. Kobra Khan caught two touchdown passes. The first came on fourth-and-five with eighteen seconds left before halftime, a direct demonstration that Sunyshore is willing to ask the passing game to decide a possession when the stakes are concentrated.

Petalburg recorded one sack against Rustboro, Parasect’s six-yard stop, and Watzon was not sacked in the wild-card round. Those separate facts make protection and pressure an important point to watch without proving an automatic matchup advantage. The Pride need enough disruption to prevent Sunyshore from using its rushing success to make every passing choice comfortable. The Starseekers need enough time for their reliable receivers to convert it.

The teams also arrive with different kicking outcomes. Petalburg’s Sunflora made both field goals and his one extra point, while the Pride added two successful two-point tries. Sunyshore’s Kayden Lyons made a fifty-six-yard field goal but missed one of three extra points. Those are recent results, not predictions of the next attempt. In a close game, the available scoring choices and the points actually collected will matter alongside the larger yardage comparisons.

There is no need to manufacture a rivalry to make this game interesting. Two division winners with different offensive scales are meeting for a conference-final berth. Petalburg has repeatedly made close games work. Sunyshore has recently won through stronger rushing and defensive performance. Each team has a current, observed method that the other must interrupt.
The injury report favors careful role accounting

Oinkologne remains listed with one week of recovery for Petalburg. He rushed for 957 yards during the regular season, so the absence removes a substantial part of the team’s earlier production. Glalie’s wild-card work provides an observed alternative, and his new minor injury entry has zero weeks remaining. The Pride can prepare around what their available backfield just accomplished without pretending the season’s leading runner has already returned.

Sunyshore’s 88 Special remains listed for fifteen weeks. The Starseekers already played their wild-card game without that earlier receiving contributor, with Fera LaGatr and Kobra Khan supplying the prominent catches. Serp Gardener, Nair Jordan and BJ Vickers have new minor entries with no remaining absence. Those designations should be carried accurately into the preview rather than converted into unsupported medical expectations.

My forecast is Sunyshore 27, Petalburg 17. I expect Gabite’s rushing and the Starseekers’ broader season-long defense to create a more sustainable scoring advantage than Rustboro managed. Petalburg’s third-down execution should keep the game competitive, but repeating six conversions in nine attempts against this opponent is a substantial demand. The Pride’s clearest upset route is to slow the ground game, keep Iron Valiant free of giveaways and preserve one last useful possession.

The winner faces Mossdeep or Dewford. Either Sunyshore or Petalburg would travel to the top-seeded Eclipse; either would host the fifth-seeded Breakers. For now, the route begins with a much smaller set of obligations: stop a productive runner, finish a third down, catch the pass that keeps a possession alive. Both clubs just advanced because enough players completed those jobs. This meeting will leave room for only one of them to do it again.

articles.title: Lapras leads a line class with more than one kind of athlete
articles.dek: The Rook Board separates twelve visible OL prospects by reported range, strength and movement, with Klawf forcing an early conversation.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: Agate State’s Lapras leads this OL board because the visible range and movement tests support the same early interest. A 77–99 range is the strongest among the selected prospects, and a 4.95 forty with a 6.91 cone gives me more than a large number to admire. I would begin the line evaluation there, then make Paniola State’s Eiscue and University of Sunyshore’s Klawf part of the same serious discussion.

Klawf is the athlete I keep returning to: twenty-one bench repetitions, a 4.86 forty and a 6.83 cone. Those are recorded combine measures, not proof that every protection snap will be clean. They are enough to make the prospect’s 65–93 range especially interesting. A team should investigate how that movement and strength fit its actual line need before treating a broad rating interval as a complete scouting report.

Torkoal and Shuckle present a different argument, with strong visible ranges and slower movement testing. I am keeping them high while asking more specific positional questions. The league lists these prospects as OL; the available scouting record does not establish a college snap history at tackle, guard or center. This board therefore does not invent one to make the rankings sound more precise.

Fortree’s rebuilding conversations and Rustboro’s next decisions should include this class, but I am not assigning a final draft position before the draft order and available choices are settled. The board is a ranking of these twelve visible prospects, not a promise that a particular club can select one. Every school assignment remains the player’s established university, including the two distinct Eiscue prospects.

The same caution applies to the range endpoints. A 99 at the top of an interval is not a revealed 99-rated player, and a strong combine does not reveal an unseen development ceiling. I have made the judgments below from the reported ranges and tests. The next useful scouting step is to reduce uncertainty about the specific job the player would be asked to perform.

prospects.name: Lapras
prospects.analysis: Lapras combines the strongest visible range, 77–99, with a 4.95 forty and 6.91 cone. Agate State’s prospect leads my board because the broad athletic case accompanies the rating range.
prospects.concern: A wide range still leaves substantial uncertainty; the combine does not establish actual pass-blocking technique.
prospects.projection: First OL on this board; a club seeking an early contributor should investigate the position fit.

prospects.name: Eiscue
prospects.analysis: Paniola State’s Eiscue pairs a 71–99 range with nineteen bench repetitions and a 6.96 cone. The strength-and-movement combination gives me a second credible top choice.
prospects.concern: The top of a visible range is a possibility, not a measured current rating.
prospects.projection: An early line target for a team balancing immediate help and further development.

prospects.name: Klawf
prospects.analysis: Klawf is my favorite movement-and-strength combination: 4.86 in the forty, twenty-one bench reps and a 6.83 cone, alongside a 65–93 range. University of Sunyshore sends an athlete I want to examine closely.
prospects.concern: Athletic testing alone cannot prove protection reliability or identify the best line position.
prospects.projection: Aggressive early consideration, particularly when movement matters to the intended role.

prospects.name: Torkoal
prospects.analysis: University of Cinnabar’s Torkoal has a 68–96 range and eighteen bench reps. The 5.21 forty and 7.24 cone make this a different athletic proposition from Klawf.
prospects.concern: Slower movement measures deserve attention before assigning an edge-protection job.
prospects.projection: A high-board strength candidate whose actual positional fit needs further checking.

prospects.name: Shuckle
prospects.analysis: University of Mauville’s Shuckle brings a 66–94 range and sixteen bench reps. I place the prospect here for the visible football range while recognizing the slower testing profile.
prospects.concern: The 7.27 cone and 5.19 forty give me less movement confidence than the names above.
prospects.projection: Early-to-middle line consideration with role-specific evaluation still essential.

prospects.name: Tropius
prospects.analysis: North Orre’s Tropius has a 63–91 range and seventeen bench reps, with a 5.06 forty. The profile is balanced enough to remain in the first group after the more striking top athletes.
prospects.concern: The 7.10 cone does not separate Tropius from several close alternatives.
prospects.projection: A credible line-building candidate when the top four are gone.

prospects.name: Audino
prospects.analysis: Saffron Tech’s Audino matches the 63–91 range and adds a 5.00 forty, sixteen bench reps and a thirty-five-inch vertical. The testing offers several useful positives without one defining outlier.
prospects.concern: A broad range prevents a confident claim of immediate starting quality.
prospects.projection: A balanced alternative for teams seeking several plausible line roles.

prospects.name: Spiritomb
prospects.analysis: Blackthorn State’s Spiritomb offers eighteen bench reps and a 59–87 range. Strength is the clearest testing reason to keep this prospect above similarly ranged alternatives.
prospects.concern: The visible data does not establish whether that strength translates to reliable blocking.
prospects.projection: A middle-board target with further technical evaluation required.

prospects.name: Eiscue
prospects.analysis: Azalea’s Eiscue runs 4.92 with seventeen bench reps and a 60–88 range. The second Eiscue on the list is a separate prospect with a different school and testing line.
prospects.concern: The 7.09 cone is less striking than the forty; do not collapse two movement tests into one conclusion.
prospects.projection: A useful alternative if the Paniola prospect is selected earlier.

prospects.name: Stunfisk
prospects.analysis: Castelia’s Stunfisk combines a 58–86 range, fifteen bench reps and a 7.00 cone. It is a steady profile within a crowded middle group.
prospects.concern: No visible measure here removes the uncertainty between a reserve and a future starter.
prospects.projection: Middle-board line depth with a plausible larger role after further evaluation.

prospects.name: Tirtouga
prospects.analysis: Gateon’s Tirtouga has a narrower 61–75 range and sixteen bench reps. That narrower reported interval is useful information even though its ceiling is below several wider-range prospects.
prospects.concern: A 7.16 cone and 5.14 forty do not make the movement case for us.
prospects.projection: A more constrained evaluation for teams preferring a clearer present range.

prospects.name: Dwebble
prospects.analysis: Vermilion Polytechnic’s Dwebble combines a 57–71 range with a 4.98 forty, 6.77 cone and thirty-seven-inch vertical. The movement testing earns a place despite the lower range.
prospects.concern: Thirteen bench reps and the lower range keep the projection below the top group.
prospects.projection: A later movement-oriented option whose role needs to justify the investment.

articles.title: Smoth’s five-week absence changes Saffron’s divisional preparation
articles.dek: Three new positive-week injuries are confirmed after the wild-card round; Mt. Silver’s bye clears one counter while several major absences continue.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Saffron has the most consequential new absence among the remaining eight teams. Emmitt Smoth is listed for five weeks after the Olivine game. He carried twice for fourteen yards in the 42–10 win. Dam Skattebo supplied the larger rushing workload, with ninety-four yards and two touchdowns, so the immediate task is to preserve that production while accounting for the missing backfield option. No replacement workload has been announced in the evidence reviewed here.

The other new positive-week injuries belong to eliminated teams: Olivine’s Magmar is listed for four weeks and Hearthome’s Palafin for two. Their entries remain part of the league-wide report even though they no longer affect a divisional matchup. The table distinguishes these new injuries from ordinary one-week reductions on older recovery counters.

Mt. Silver’s bye brought Ninji Asomugha’s counter to zero. Tic Thorpe still has two weeks reported, Josh Alakazam three, Tony Gyarzalez four and Vibrava four. Ariados remains at nine and Medicham at three. The Reds face Hatterene’s Blackthorn passing game with several continuing absences; a cleared counter for Asomugha does not establish the exact defensive lineup.

Blackthorn’s Exploud also reached zero, while Sawsbuck remains at three weeks. Lavender’s Mr. Clanky remains at four. Mossdeep’s Poury Holt remains at five, Sunyshore’s 88 Special at fifteen, and Petalburg’s Oinkologne at one. The last of those is particularly relevant to a game against Sunyshore’s productive rushing attack: the Pride’s available backfield just won with Glalie and Whiscash, while its 957-yard regular-season runner still carries a positive counter.

Several important players received new minor entries with zero remaining weeks, including Saffron’s HeeDee Lamb and Pach Tatum, Sunyshore’s Serp Gardener, Nair Jordan and BJ Vickers, and Petalburg’s Glalie. These entries do not support an invented missed game or a questionable designation. Dewford’s Dusclops and Lavender’s Vikavolt and Axew are in the same zero-week category.

Reported weeks describe the current injury record. A reduction is recovery progress, not a newly suffered injury. A cleared designation establishes neither an appearance nor a starting role, and a healthy player still on injured reserve requires an actual roster move before that status changes. Game reports do not supply reliable injury timestamps, so this report does not assign an injury to a particular play.

articles.title: The remaining eight: Blackthorn makes the largest new claim
articles.dek: A postseason-only ranking after the wild-card round, with the final thirty-two-team regular-season list preserved in the archive.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: The field is down to eight, and this ranking covers those eight. The final regular-season ranking remains in the playoff-launch issue; eliminated clubs have not been quietly erased from that historical list. This is my current order of the remaining championship contenders, weighing the full season, the wild-card performance and confirmed availability.

Blackthorn gives me the strongest reason to move a team upward in my current assessment. Hatterene threw five touchdown passes on the road, and the Dragons now revisit a top seed they already beat. Mt. Silver’s injuries make that matchup more difficult than its bye might suggest. Mossdeep remains first, Saffron second, and Sunyshore’s controlled win keeps it above the newly explosive Dragons.

Mara went six-for-six on wild-card winners. The rest of us will be accepting her conversation choices for at least one meeting. Her opening bracket remains intact through the first round; Ellis’s Cinnabar championship path is eliminated. Every original bracket remains available exactly as published, while the current panel makes new round-specific judgments.

rankings.text: Seventeen wins, 724 points scored and 130 allowed remain the strongest complete-season case. The late rest policy changes how we read the finale lineups, while Dewford’s earlier 24–21 loss supplies an actual reason for the Eclipse to pay attention. Marino, Accel BeckhmJr and Ninjaskamara give Mossdeep several established scoring routes. I keep them first until the playoff evidence changes that.

The last four scores are 70, 31, 49 and 42. Olivine led briefly, then conceded thirty-five unanswered points. Manning, Lamb, Skattebo and Slampert all supplied touchdowns in different ways. Smoth’s five-week absence is a real cost, but Saffron retains its main rushing and receiving production. Lavender’s return game is the next detail that needs more respect than a comfortable final score might encourage.

Myles Gabite rushed for 106 yards while Hearthome managed nineteen as a team. Watzon took no sacks and threw no interceptions. That is a persuasive way to move past the loss at Mossdeep and into a home divisional game. Petalburg’s third-down offense will be a harder finishing test, but Sunyshore has an inviting ground-game comparison after the Pride allowed 163 rushing yards to Rustboro.

Five touchdown passes at Cinnabar and a previous 30–22 win at Mt. Silver make the Dragons much more than a fifth-seed inconvenience. Their 70–0 loss at Saffron still belongs in the season record, and their defense allowed 348 regular-season points. I am ranking current remaining contenders, so Hatterene’s actual road response gets substantial weight without erasing those vulnerabilities.

rankings.themeLabel: The bye did not clear everyone
rankings.text: The Reds earned the top seed and have Garshawn Lynch’s 1,200-yard rushing season. They also still have positive recovery counters for Tic Thorpe, Josh Alakazam, Tony Gyarzalez and several others. Blackthorn already won here. Mt. Silver can answer through sustained rushing and home execution, but the current available passing group leaves more uncertainty than its regular-season record alone suggests.

Hobbes’s seventy-three-yard return was magnificent. Lavender still gained only 218 offensive yards while allowing 368 to Vermilion. Both facts belong in the ranking. The Wails have earned nine consecutive wins and a trip to Saffron; their next improvement needs to be in ordinary possessions, because another enormous late return cannot be scheduled on the preparation sheet.

The Breakers have won four straight and held Eterna without a touchdown. Watchog finished two short rushing opportunities, and Carnivine supplied the late interception. Dewford also came within three of Mossdeep earlier in the season. Its 105-yard wild-card passing game makes a large early deficit dangerous, but its current availability and several recent routes to victory give it a legitimate upset argument.

Glameow and Magneton gained eighteen receiving yards between them, all on the final touchdown drive. Petalburg converted six of nine third downs and finished its opportunities with two successful two-point tries. The Pride also allowed 163 rushing yards, which puts Myles Gabite near the top of the next meeting agenda. Eighth among the remaining eight still means the club has earned another game.

Mara went 6–0 in the wild-card round; Ellis and I went 5–1, while Rowan and Dorian went 4–2. Those records count winners. Closest-score bonuses remain separate, and nobody predicted an exact final score. Mara’s six correct calls included both Blackthorn and Petalburg.

picks.author: tessa-wren
picks.reason: I expect Gabite and the Starseekers’ rushing attack to sustain drives while the defense reduces Petalburg’s six-of-nine third-down rate. Oinkologne’s continuing absence makes it harder for the Pride to create an equally reliable ground answer.
